source: claude-architect-exam-guide (github.com/utkarsh1agarwal) — original questions written against the public CCAR-F blueprint

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude to "clean up this parsing function" with no further detail. Three separate attempts produce three meaningfully different refactors, each reasonable in isolation but inconsistent with each other. What is the most effective way to converge on a consistent result?
options: Reduce max_tokens so the model has less room to improvise
Ask for five more attempts and pick the best one
Repeat the same request with stronger emphasis ("please be consistent this time")
Provide 2–3 concrete before/after examples showing exactly what "cleaned up" means for this codebase's style
questions.why: — Three inconsistent refactors from the same vague instruction is a definitional-ambiguity problem, not a randomness problem, so 2–3 concrete before/after examples pinning down what "cleaned up" means fixes the actual cause. Reducing max_tokens or repeating the request with more emphasis doesn't resolve what "clean" means for this codebase.

questions.stem: Before implementing a rate-limiting feature in a service Claude hasn't seen before, a developer wants Claude to first ask about traffic patterns, failure behavior under load, and whether limits should be per-user or global. What technique does this describe, and when is it most valuable?
options: Prompt chaining — valuable for any multi-step task regardless of familiarity
Plan mode — but only for single-file changes
Test-driven iteration — valuable only when a test suite already exists
The interview pattern — most valuable in unfamiliar domains where the developer may not have anticipated key design considerations
questions.why: — Asking Claude to surface traffic-pattern, failure-mode, and scoping questions before writing any code is the interview pattern, and it earns its keep specifically in unfamiliar domains where the developer hasn't already anticipated every design consideration. Prompt chaining (A) sequences already-known steps rather than surfacing unknown design questions.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to build a data-migration script and has already written a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases (including null values), and performance constraints. What is the recommended way to use these tests during development?
options: Show Claude the tests once at the start, then ignore test results during implementation
Iterate by sharing test failures with Claude after each attempt, letting it progressively correct the implementation
Convert the tests into prose requirements instead of running them
Withhold the tests until the implementation is "done" so Claude isn't biased toward passing them narrowly
questions.why: — With tests already covering behavior, edge cases, and performance up front, the recommended loop is to hand Claude the actual failures after each attempt so it can progressively converge. Showing tests once and then ignoring results (A), or withholding them until "done" (D), both break the feedback loop that makes test-driven iteration work.

questions.stem: A pull request fixes three bugs that interact — fixing bug 1 changes the correct approach to fixing bug 2. Which approach to communicating these to Claude is better?
options: Report each bug in a separate message, waiting for a fix before mentioning the next
Only describe the most severe bug and let Claude discover the other two independently
Ask Claude to guess which bugs might be related before describing any of them
Describe all three interacting issues together in one detailed message
questions.why: — Because fixing bug 1 changes the correct approach to bug 2, the issues interact, and interacting issues must be described together in one detailed message so Claude reasons about them jointly. Reporting them one at a time (A) risks Claude fixing bug 2 in a way bug 1's fix later invalidates, forcing rework.

questions.stem: A team is deciding between a single-file bug fix (clear stack trace, one obvious cause) and a cross-service authentication redesign (multiple valid approaches, dozens of files). Which pairing is correct?
options: Direct execution for the bug fix; plan mode for the authentication redesign
Plan mode for both, since plan mode is always safer
Direct execution for both, since Claude Code doesn't meaningfully benefit from planning
Plan mode for the bug fix; direct execution for the redesign
questions.why: — A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace is the well-understood, low-ambiguity case direct execution suits, while a cross-service redesign with multiple valid approaches and dozens of files benefits from planning before committing to changes. Treating plan mode as "always safer" (B) ignores the needless overhead it adds on trivial, unambiguous fixes.

questions.stem: A /deploy-check slash command should run the team's pre-deployment checklist and be available to every developer immediately after cloning the repo. Where should it live?
options: .claude/commands/deploy-check.md in the repository
A .claude/config.json commands array
~/.claude/commands/deploy-check.md
Inside the root CLAUDE.md file as a named section
questions.why: — A command every developer needs immediately after cloning must be version-controlled and project-scoped, which is exactly what .claude/commands/deploy-check.md provides. The personal ~/.claude/commands/ location (C) is never shared via git, so a fresh clone wouldn't have it.

questions.stem: A "brainstorm alternative approaches" skill tends to produce long, exploratory output that isn't useful to keep in the main conversation once a decision is made. Which frontmatter setting addresses this?
options: context: fork
allowed-tools
paths
argument-hint
questions.why: — context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, keeping the long exploratory brainstorm output out of the main conversation once a decision is made. allowed-tools (B) restricts which tools a skill can call, not where its output lands.

questions.stem: Two engineers on the same team have different personal preferences for commit-message style, but the team's actual required conventions live correctly in the project-level CLAUDE.md. One engineer also has their personal preferences saved in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What's true about this setup?
options: It's broken — user-level and project-level CLAUDE.md files cannot coexist
It's fine — the user-level file applies only to that engineer and doesn't affect teammates via version control
Only one CLAUDE.md file can be active per repository
The user-level file will silently overwrite the project-level file for everyone
questions.why: — User-level and project-level CLAUDE.md files are designed to coexist and stack; the personal file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is never checked into version control, so it only affects that one engineer's own sessions. Claiming it "silently overwrites" the project file for everyone (D) misreads the hierarchy — personal preferences layer on top of, rather than replace, shared team conventions.

questions.stem: A large monorepo has different testing conventions for unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests, each identifiable by filename pattern but scattered across many directories. What's the best way to load the right convention automatically based on which file is being edited?
options: Three separate skills that must be manually invoked before editing each test type
Three separate directory-level CLAUDE.md files, duplicated into every directory containing tests
One root CLAUDE.md with three sections and hope Claude infers the right one
Three separate .claude/rules/*.md files, each with paths frontmatter matching the relevant filename pattern
questions.why: — Because each convention is tied to a filename pattern rather than a single directory, three .claude/rules/*.md files with paths frontmatter load automatically based on which file is being edited, regardless of location. Duplicating directory-level CLAUDE.md files into every test directory (B) doesn't scale and invites drift.

questions.stem: A developer wants to compare two different caching strategies starting from the same point in their investigation of a codebase, without redoing the initial exploration twice. What capability supports this?
options: --resume with two different session names created independently
/compact run twice
fork_session, branching two parallel explorations from the shared baseline
Restarting from scratch for each strategy
questions.why: — fork_session is built for exactly this: branching two parallel explorations from a shared baseline so the initial investigation isn't redone. Using --resume with two independently created session names (A) doesn't share a common starting point the way a fork does.

questions.stem: A developer resumes a two-day-old session to continue a refactor, but teammates modified several of the files Claude had already analyzed in that session. Claude's suggestions reference outdated function signatures. What should have been done?
options: Used fork_session instead of --resume
Started an entirely new session with zero context
Informed the resumed session explicitly about which files changed, prompting targeted re-analysis
Increased max_tokens for the resumed session
questions.why: — Resuming a session doesn't make Claude aware that files changed since last time; the fix is explicitly telling it which files changed so it can do targeted re-analysis. Switching to fork_session (A) solves a different problem (parallel branching), not stale context in a resumed session.

questions.stem: A skill for generating boilerplate files should never be allowed to run destructive shell commands, even accidentally. Which frontmatter field enforces this restriction directly?
options: argument-hint
paths
context: fork
allowed-tools
questions.why: — allowed-tools frontmatter directly restricts which tools a skill can invoke, so scoping it away from shell/Bash access structurally prevents destructive commands. context: fork (C) isolates output/context, it doesn't restrict tool access.

questions.stem: A developer needs to trace how a specific exported utility function is used across a codebase, including through re-export wrapper modules with different names. What's the most effective approach?
options: First identify all exported names for the function (including wrapper re-exports), then Grep for each name across the codebase
Read every file in the repository upfront to build full context before searching
Glob for /*.ts and manually scan the output
Ask the user to supply the call sites manually
questions.why: — Wrapper re-exports mean the function may be called under several different names, so all of them must be enumerated before Grep can find every call site; grepping only the original name would miss usages through renamed re-exports. Reading every file upfront (B) is the anti-pattern the built-in exploration pattern warns against — start with targeted search, not full reads.

questions.stem: During a long exploration session tracing a legacy codebase's dependency graph, Claude starts giving vague answers referencing "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it examined 90 minutes earlier. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase max_tokens on each subsequent call
Switch to a different underlying model mid-session
Have the agent maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings, and reference it for subsequent questions
Restart with zero context and re-explore from scratch
questions.why: — Vague "typical patterns" answers after 90 minutes of exploration signal context degradation, not a capacity problem, so a scratchpad file persisting specific findings (the classes actually examined) directly counters it. Increasing max_tokens (A) doesn't address the model losing track of specifics it already found.

questions.stem: A task requires exploring an unfamiliar codebase's structure without exhausting the main session's context on verbose file-by-file discovery output. Which capability is designed for this?
options: fork_session
/memory
The Explore subagent
context: fork applied to CLAUDE.md
questions.why: — The Explore subagent isolates verbose file-by-file discovery output during structure-mapping tasks, so the main session's context isn't exhausted by exploration noise. fork_session (A) is for branching parallel investigations from a shared point, not for keeping exploration noise out of the main session in the first place.

questions.stem: A CI job runs claude "Review this PR for security issues" and hangs indefinitely. What's the fix?
options: Redirect /dev/null into stdin
claude -p "Review this PR for security issues"
Set CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true as an environment variable
Add a --batch flag
questions.why: — claude -p "..." runs non-interactively, which is exactly what prevents a CI job from blocking while waiting on a stdin prompt. A (piping /dev/null) is a hacky workaround at best, and C/D reference an env var and flag that don't actually exist — classic plausible-but-fictional distractors.

questions.stem: The team wants automated review findings posted as individual inline PR comments by a script, requiring machine-parseable output rather than free-form prose. Which combination of flags supports this?
options: --resume with a named session
-p alone is sufficient
fork_session for each file reviewed
--output-format json combined with --json-schema
questions.why: — --output-format json combined with --json-schema forces genuinely schema-compliant, machine-parseable findings a script can split into individual inline comments. -p alone (B) only makes the run non-interactive; it says nothing about the shape of the output.

questions.stem: A CI pipeline re-runs code review after each new commit to a PR, and developers complain about receiving duplicate comments for issues already flagged (and already acknowledged as "won't fix") in the previous run. What should change?
options: Disable review entirely after the first commit
Nothing — duplicate comments are unavoidable with automated review
Include prior review findings in context on re-runs, and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
Switch to --output-format json only, without changing the prompt
questions.why: — Feeding prior review findings (including ones already dismissed as "won't fix") into context and instructing Claude to report only new/unaddressed issues fixes the actual root cause: each re-run currently has no memory of what was already flagged. Disabling review (A) or shrugging off duplicates as unavoidable (B) discard the tool's value instead of fixing the re-run design.

questions.stem: A CI-triggered test-generation step keeps suggesting test cases that duplicate scenarios already covered in the existing test suite. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase the model's max_tokens for test generation
Run test generation twice and manually deduplicate
Provide the existing test files in context so generation avoids already-covered scenarios
Switch to a different CI runner
questions.why: — Providing the existing test files in context directly closes the information gap causing redundant suggestions — the model simply can't avoid duplicating coverage it can't see. Running generation twice and manually deduping (B) treats the symptom while doubling cost.

questions.stem: The same Claude Code session that generated a bug fix is also used, immediately afterward, to review that fix before merge — and subtle logic errors keep slipping through to a human reviewer instead. What's the underlying issue?
options: The context window is too small to hold both the fix and the review
The session retains reasoning from generation and is less likely to challenge its own prior decisions; use an independent instance for review
--output-format json wasn't enabled during review
The prompt needs more few-shot examples of what bugs look like
questions.why: — The session retains its own generation reasoning and is structurally less inclined to challenge decisions it just made, so an independent review instance is the fix — not a config flag (C) or more few-shot examples (D). This exact pattern shows up in both the CI/CD-workflow material and the multi-instance-review material, so it genuinely straddles both domains rather than being a clean D3-vs-D4 call.

questions.stem: Your CI system wants Claude to auto-generate high-value tests rather than generic boilerplate assertions. What should be documented in CLAUDE.md to improve this?
options: The CI provider's internal infrastructure details
Testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures/conventions
The full list of every function in the codebase
Nothing — test quality is purely a function of model capability
questions.why: — Documenting testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and available fixtures/conventions in CLAUDE.md gives the model the missing project-specific judgment it needs to generate high-value tests instead of boilerplate. Dumping every function (C) or citing CI infra details (A) doesn't address what makes a test worth writing.

questions.stem: A 14-file PR review produces contradictory findings — a pattern flagged as a bug in one file and approved as fine in another file within the same PR. What's the best structural fix?
options: Use a model with a larger context window and re-run as a single pass
Require three full-PR passes and keep majority-vote findings
Ask developers to manually pre-split the PR into under-4-file chunks
Split the review into focused per-file passes for local issues, plus a separate cross-file integration pass
questions.why: — Splitting into focused per-file passes for local issues plus a separate cross-file integration pass directly fixes the attention-dilution problem causing contradictory findings across a 14-file review. A bigger model in a single pass (A) or brute-force majority voting across three full-PR passes (B) don't address the structural cause; offloading the split to developers (C) isn't a tooling fix at all.

questions.stem: A team wants to move their nightly automated code-review job for main (no human waiting on results) to reduce API costs. Which approach fits, and why?
options: Message Batches API — it's non-blocking and latency-tolerant, well suited to overnight jobs, at 50% lower cost
Message Batches API is inappropriate here since it lacks multi-turn tool calling
Batch it, but only if a real-time SLA under one hour can be guaranteed
Keep it fully synchronous, since batch jobs cannot run unattended
questions.why: — An unattended overnight job with no one waiting on results is exactly the non-blocking, latency-tolerant case the Message Batches API is built for, at roughly 50% lower cost. B is wrong since multi-turn tool calling isn't needed for a review job like this, and C/D impose constraints (SLA guarantee, staying synchronous) that don't apply to an unattended nightly run.

questions.stem: Developers report that automated review flags a specific pattern as a "style" issue 40% of the time incorrectly, eroding trust in the tool overall — including in categories that are actually accurate. What should be done?
options: Turn off all automated review categories permanently
Nothing; false positives in one category don't affect trust in others
Add "please be more careful" to the prompt
Define explicit criteria for that category and consider temporarily disabling it while iterating, to protect trust in the accurate categories
questions.why: — A 40%-false-positive category is actively eroding trust in categories that are accurate, so defining explicit criteria for that category (and considering temporarily disabling it while iterating) protects overall trust in the tool. Vague reinforcement like "be more careful" (C) doesn't fix ill-defined criteria, and permanently killing all categories (A) overcorrects.

questions.stem: A CI review prompt currently says "flag anything that seems off." What change would most reduce false positives?
options: Require unanimous agreement from three separate runs before flagging anything
Add "only flag things you're very confident about"
Lower the sampling temperature to 0
Replace the vague instruction with specific, categorical criteria (e.g., "flag a comment only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior")
questions.why: — Replacing "flag anything that seems off" with specific, categorical criteria (e.g., claimed vs. actual behavior contradiction) removes the ambiguity that vague instructions can't resolve. "Only flag things you're very confident about" (B) is exactly the kind of vague reinforcement that's been shown not to reduce false positives.

questions.stem: A CI pipeline needs Claude to generate a PR summary, then a set of suggested reviewers, then a risk score — as three separate, dependent steps where each step's output feeds the next. Which pattern best matches this?
options: fork_session to branch each step independently
Parallel subagent spawning via the Task tool
Dynamic/adaptive decomposition, since the steps are open-ended
Prompt chaining — a fixed sequential pipeline of well-understood, ordered steps
questions.why: — Three fixed, ordered, well-understood steps where each output feeds the next is the textbook definition of prompt chaining, not open-ended/adaptive decomposition (C), which is for investigations where next steps depend on unknown findings.

questions.stem: Which CLI flag is specifically intended to prevent a CI job from hanging on interactive prompts?
options: --resume
--json-schema
-p / --print
--output-format
questions.why: — -p / --print is specifically the non-interactive mode flag that prevents hanging on stdin in a CI context; the other options control output formatting or session continuity, not interactivity.

questions.stem: A batch code-review job covering 500 files returns partial failures. What's the correct remediation?
options: Discard failed files permanently, since batches can't be retried
Identify failures by custom_id and resubmit only those, adjusting for the specific failure cause
Switch the entire job to synchronous calls going forward
Resubmit the entire batch of 500 files
questions.why: — Batch requests correlate to responses via custom_id, so failures can be precisely identified and only those resubmitted with an adjustment for the specific cause. Discarding failures (A) or resubmitting the full 500-file batch (D) wastes cost and ignores the correlation mechanism the API provides for exactly this situation.

questions.stem: A CI test-generation job has an SLA requiring results within 30 hours of PR creation, using the Message Batches API's 24-hour processing window. How should submission timing be handled?
options: Submit at a frequency (e.g., every 4–6 hours) that guarantees any given PR's batch completes within the 24-hour window, leaving buffer against the 30-hour SLA
Switch to real-time calls entirely, since batch has no SLA guarantee
Submit immediately when the PR opens and hope it completes in time
Submit only once daily at midnight regardless of PR volume
questions.why: — Since the Batches API offers no latency SLA within its up-to-24-hour window, submitting on a cadence (e.g., every 4-6 hours) bounds worst-case wait-before-submission plus processing time comfortably under the 30-hour deadline. Submitting immediately "and hoping" (C) or batching only once daily regardless of volume (D) either lacks a deliberate buffer or risks a PR opened right after the daily cutoff blowing the SLA.

questions.stem: 30. (Select TWO) Which two statements about the Message Batches API are accurate?
options: It offers roughly 50% cost savings compared to synchronous calls
Batch requests are correlated to responses using session names via --resume
Processing may take up to 24 hours, with no guaranteed latency SLA
It supports multi-turn tool calling within a single batch request
questions.why: — The Batches API gives ~50% cost savings (A) and processes within an up-to-24-hour window with no guaranteed latency SLA (C). B is wrong because correlation uses custom_id, not session names/--resume, and D is wrong because multi-turn tool calling mid-request isn't supported in a single batch call.

questions.stem: Production logs show the agent skips get_customer in 15% of cases when the customer volunteers their name, occasionally leading to an incorrect account being modified. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Add few-shot examples showing correct verification order
Build a routing classifier to detect which tools are relevant per request
Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order/process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID
Strengthen the system prompt's wording around verification being "mandatory"
questions.why: — This mirrors the classic verify-before-refund anti-pattern: a probabilistic fix (better wording, few-shot examples) still leaves a non-zero failure rate on a task with account-modification consequences, so only a structural prerequisite hook can guarantee get_customer runs first. D sounds intuitive but "mandatory" language is exactly the kind of prompt-only fix that produced the 15% failure rate in the first place.

questions.stem: A support agent has tools get_customer and lookup_order with minimal descriptions, and misroutes order-status questions to get_customer. What should be tried first, before adding few-shot examples or restructuring tools?
options: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, and explicit boundaries distinguishing the two
Build a pre-processing keyword router
Merge the tools into one generic tool
Force tool_choice to always select lookup_order
questions.why: — Tool description quality is the primary, lowest-effort lever for tool-selection accuracy and should always be tried before few-shot examples, routing layers, or restructuring. Merging (C) or forcing a single tool (D) are overcorrections that break legitimate use cases for the other tool.

questions.stem: A PostToolUse hook is used to convert lookup_order's Unix timestamps and get_customer's ISO 8601 dates into one consistent format before the model reasons about them. What category of problem does this solve?
options: Tool selection ambiguity
Data-format inconsistency across tools feeding into the model's context
Batch request correlation
Escalation calibration
questions.why: — Normalizing heterogeneous timestamp/date formats via a PostToolUse hook is precisely a data-format consistency fix so the model reasons over clean, comparable values instead of misinterpreting formats; it isn't about which tool to call (A) or escalation (D).

questions.stem: A refund-processing hook blocks any process_refund call above $500 and redirects to escalate_to_human. Which statement correctly characterizes this design choice?
options: It only works if paired with the Message Batches API
It provides deterministic, guaranteed enforcement of a business rule that a prompt alone cannot guarantee
It should be replaced by a confidence-score threshold instead
It's unnecessary since the system prompt already states the $500 limit
questions.why: — A pre-call hook that blocks and redirects above a dollar threshold provides deterministic enforcement independent of model behavior, whereas the system prompt alone (D) or a confidence-score threshold (C) only reduce, not eliminate, the failure rate on a rule with real financial consequences.

questions.stem: A multi-issue customer message (a billing dispute and a delivery delay) is handled by resolving only the first-mentioned issue and silently dropping the second. What's the correct decomposition approach instead?
options: Ask the customer to resend their message with only one issue at a time
Randomly pick which issue to address based on severity keywords
Escalate immediately since multi-issue messages are too complex
Decompose into the distinct items, investigate each with shared context, then synthesize one unified resolution covering both
questions.why: — Multi-issue requests need decomposition into distinct items, investigation of each with shared context, then a single synthesized resolution — mirroring the per-item-then-synthesis pattern used elsewhere in task decomposition. Silently dropping or randomly prioritizing one issue (B) or offloading the problem to the customer (A) both abandon the second issue instead of resolving it.

questions.stem: lookup_order returns multiple matching orders for the identifiers given. What's the correct handling, and why?
options: Escalate immediately without attempting disambiguation
Process the request against the first match returned
Ask for an additional identifier to disambiguate, rather than guessing
Select heuristically (e.g., most recent), since customers usually mean their latest order
questions.why: — Multiple ambiguous matches call for requesting an additional identifier rather than guessing; picking the "most recent" (D) or first result (B) risks acting on the wrong account/order, which is exactly the kind of identity/data risk this domain flags as needing disambiguation, not heuristics.

questions.stem: When escalating a case to a human agent who has no access to the conversation transcript, what should the structured handoff include?
options: Just a one-line description of the customer's mood
Only the ticket's timestamp
The full raw conversation log, unformatted, with no summary
Customer details, root cause analysis, and a recommended action
questions.why: — Since the human has no transcript access, the handoff must substitute for that missing context: customer details, root cause, and a recommended action. A raw, unformatted transcript (C) reintroduces the token-bloat problem instead of giving the human an actionable summary.

questions.stem: An agent is given 18 tools spanning billing, shipping, loyalty programs, and account management, and tool-selection accuracy for its core support tasks has dropped. What's the most appropriate fix?
options: Add more few-shot examples covering every possible tool combination
Force tool_choice: "any" to guarantee some tool gets called
Increase max_tokens for reasoning about tool choice
Scope the agent to only the 4–6 tools relevant to its actual role
questions.why: — Scoping the agent to the 4–6 tools relevant to its actual role directly addresses selection-accuracy degradation caused by tool-list bloat; adding more few-shot examples (A) doesn't fix the root over-provisioning problem and doesn't scale to every combination of 18 tools.

questions.stem: A lookup_order call fails due to a backend timeout. Which response correctly distinguishes this from a valid empty result?
options: Return a generic "no data" string
Return isError: true with errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true, and a description of what was attempted
Return an empty array and mark the call successful
Silently retry forever without informing the coordinator/caller
questions.why: — A backend timeout is an access failure, not a valid empty result, so it must be reported with isError: true, a transient category, retryability, and context on what was attempted — conflating it with an empty-but-successful result (C) hides a recoverable failure from the coordinator.

questions.stem: First-contact resolution sits at 55% against an 80% target; logs show the agent escalates simple, well-evidenced cases while attempting to autonomously resolve cases that actually require policy exceptions. What's the most effective fix?
options: A separately trained ML classifier on historical tickets
Self-reported confidence-score routing
Sentiment-based escalation
Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing escalate-vs-resolve cases
questions.why: — The described failure (escalating easy cases, autonomously resolving cases needing policy exceptions) is a criteria-calibration problem, best fixed with explicit escalate-vs-resolve criteria and few-shot examples; confidence scores (B) and sentiment (C) are both known-unreliable proxies for actual case complexity.

questions.stem: A 20-turn support conversation is progressively summarized, and a specific dollar amount and order number mentioned early on are lost from the summary by turn 18, causing the agent to ask the customer to repeat themselves. What's the direct fix?
options: Increase the context window size
Disable summarization for the whole conversation
Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (amount, order ID, dates) that rides along outside the summarized narrative
Ask the customer to restate key facts every turn as a matter of policy
questions.why: — A persistent case-facts block for hard data (amounts, order IDs, dates) that rides outside the summarized narrative directly prevents progressive summarization from dropping numbers the agent needs later. Disabling summarization entirely (B) or expanding the context window (A) don't address the actual mechanism of loss.

questions.stem: A customer explicitly and calmly states, "Please transfer me to a human," at the very start of an otherwise simple, resolvable interaction. What should happen?
options: Attempt to resolve the issue first, since it appears simple, then transfer if the customer insists again
Offer an incentive to keep the customer with the automated agent
Escalate immediately, honoring the explicit request without first attempting investigation
Ask why they want a human before proceeding either way
questions.why: — An explicit, calm request for a human should be honored immediately without first attempting resolution, per the escalation-trigger rule that explicit requests bypass investigation regardless of how simple the issue looks. Option A's "try to resolve first" directly violates that honor-the-explicit-request principle.

questions.stem: Which best describes the risk of using self-reported model confidence scores as the primary escalation trigger?
options: Confidence scores can't be produced without context: fork
Self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated — the model can be confidently wrong precisely on the hardest cases
Confidence scores require the Message Batches API
Confidence scores are computationally expensive to generate
questions.why: — Self-reported confidence is a poorly calibrated signal — models can be confidently wrong precisely on the hardest, most nuanced cases — which is why it's listed as an unreliable escalation trigger. The other options (batches API, context: fork, compute cost) are irrelevant technical distractors.

questions.stem: A policy document addresses refund exceptions for damaged goods but says nothing about refund exceptions for goods lost in transit. A customer requests exactly this kind of exception. What should the agent do?
options: Apply the damaged-goods policy by analogy without escalating
Deny the request since it isn't explicitly authorized
Approve the request since it isn't explicitly denied
Escalate, since this is a policy gap rather than a straightforward case
questions.why: — A policy that is silent on the specific scenario (lost-in-transit) is a genuine policy gap, and the correct trigger for silence/ambiguity is escalation — not extending policy by analogy (A) or unilaterally denying/approving (B, C) a case the policy never addressed.

questions.stem: 45. (Select TWO) Which two of the following are appropriate, reliable escalation triggers per the exam blueprint?
options: The customer explicitly requests a human agent
The policy is silent or ambiguous on the customer's specific request
The agent's self-reported confidence drops below an arbitrary threshold
The customer's message contains negative sentiment keywords
questions.why: — An explicit request for a human should always be honored, and policy silence/ambiguity is a genuine reason to escalate rather than guess. Self-reported confidence (C) and sentiment keywords (D) are both poorly-calibrated proxies for actual case complexity.

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline validates against a JSON schema and a required field, purchase_order_number, fails validation because it's missing. Investigation confirms the source invoice genuinely never included a PO number. What's the correct interpretation?
options: Increase max_tokens and retry
This retry is unlikely to succeed since the information doesn't exist in the source; the field should be nullable instead of required
Retry with the same prompt; missing-field errors are always retry-fixable
The schema needs a stricter type constraint
questions.why: — The invoice genuinely never had a PO number, so no amount of retrying manufactures data that isn't in the source; the fix is upstream, making the field nullable. Increasing max_tokens (A) or retrying the same prompt (C) can't invent missing information, and a stricter type constraint (D) doesn't address absence.

questions.stem: A validation-retry loop needs to correct a structural JSON error (a nested array flattened incorrectly) on the second attempt. What should the follow-up prompt include?
options: Nothing — tool_use with schemas should never produce structural errors, so no retry should be needed
The original document, the failed extraction output, and the specific validation error describing the structural mismatch
A brand-new, unrelated example document
Only a repeated instruction to "format correctly this time"
questions.why: — A structural error like a flattened array is retry-fixable, but only if the follow-up gives new information to correct against: the original document, the failed output, and the specific validation error. Repeating "format correctly" (D) or an unrelated example (C) provides no diagnostic signal, and assuming schema-enforced tools can never produce structural errors (A) is false.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes what tool_use with a JSON schema does and does not guarantee?
options: It guarantees semantic correctness but not syntactic validity
It guarantees syntactic (schema-compliant) validity but not semantic correctness (e.g., values landing in the wrong field or totals not summing)
It guarantees neither, and offers no benefit over plain-text JSON output
It guarantees both syntactic validity and semantic correctness of extracted values
questions.why: — tool_use with a schema guarantees the output parses and matches the schema's structure (syntactic validity) but cannot verify that values are semantically correct, e.g., a total that doesn't sum or a value in the wrong field. D overclaims that semantic correctness is also guaranteed, which is exactly the gap a calculated_total vs. stated_total check exists to catch.

questions.stem: An enum field for expense category needs to remain useful even as new, unanticipated categories appear in documents over time. What schema pattern handles this well?
options: Multiple boolean flags, one per possible category
A required string field with no enum constraint at all
A closed enum with no fallback option
An enum with an "other" value paired with a free-text category_detail field
questions.why: — Pairing an "other" enum value with a free-text category_detail field lets the schema absorb novel categories without breaking validation while still capturing detail. A closed enum (C) breaks on any new category, dropping the enum (B) sacrifices validation entirely, and per-category booleans (A) can't scale to unanticipated categories.

questions.stem: Which best describes the purpose of a detected_pattern field attached to each automated finding in a review or extraction pipeline?
options: It determines whether tool_choice should be "auto" or "any"
It stores the model's self-reported confidence
It enables systematic downstream analysis of which specific patterns trigger findings, useful for spotting recurring false-positive causes
It flags whether a finding is retryable
questions.why: — Tagging findings with the specific pattern that triggered them turns one-off fixes into an aggregate signal for spotting recurring false-positive causes. It's unrelated to tool_choice (A), isn't a confidence score (B), and doesn't indicate retryability (D).

questions.stem: Few-shot examples are added to an extraction prompt specifically to handle documents with varied structures — some using inline citations, others using bibliographies, some embedding methodology details inline versus in a separate section. What is the main benefit?
options: They demonstrate correct handling of structural variety, helping the model generalize to formats not explicitly shown
They guarantee the model will never omit a field
They eliminate the need for a JSON schema entirely
Few-shot examples primarily reduce token usage
questions.why: — Showing a few examples across genuinely different document structures teaches the underlying judgment (how to locate methodology or citations regardless of layout), letting the model generalize to formats not explicitly shown. Few-shot examples don't guarantee zero omissions (B), don't replace schema enforcement (C), and typically add tokens rather than reduce them (D).

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline is being scaled from a 20-document pilot to a 5,000-document production run using the Message Batches API. What should happen before the full run?
options: Switch to synchronous calls for the full run instead of batch
Submit all 5,000 immediately to save time
Refine the prompt against a smaller sample set first to maximize first-pass success and reduce costly iterative resubmission at scale
Skip validation entirely for the full run since the pilot already passed
questions.why: — At 5,000-document scale with batch turnaround up to 24 hours and no latency SLA, discovering a prompt flaw only after the full run is enormously costly, so refining against a smaller sample first maximizes first-pass success. Submitting everything immediately (B) or skipping validation (D) both forfeit the cheap chance to catch systematic errors early, and abandoning batch (A) throws away the reason for using it.

questions.stem: A stakeholder wants to know if a 96% aggregate extraction accuracy is good enough to safely reduce human review across the board. What should be checked first?
options: The average length of the source documents
Accuracy broken down by document type and by individual field, since aggregate numbers can mask segment-specific failure
Whether --json-schema was used during extraction
Nothing further; 96% aggregate is a strong number on its own
questions.why: — A 96% aggregate can hide a document type or field performing far worse, so only a by-type, by-field breakdown reveals whether review can safely be reduced broadly or only for specific segments. Document length (A) and whether a schema flag was used (C) don't address the masking risk, and accepting the aggregate at face value (D) is the exact mistake stratified analysis prevents.

questions.stem: Field-level confidence scores are used to route low-confidence extractions to human reviewers with limited capacity. What should determine the confidence threshold used for routing?
options: Calibration against a labeled validation set so the threshold maps to actual accuracy
The number of required fields in the schema
The size of the review team, independent of accuracy data
An arbitrary round number chosen for simplicity
questions.why: — A threshold is only meaningful if tied to what confidence level actually predicts correctness, which requires calibration against labeled ground truth. Sizing it to schema field count (B), team headcount (C), or an arbitrary round number (D) fits the threshold to convenience rather than actual error risk.

questions.stem: Two extracted values for the same metric conflict because they come from two source documents published a year apart, representing a genuine change over time rather than an error. What structured field, if present, would have prevented this from being misread as a contradiction?
options: Publication or data-collection date fields on each extracted value
isRetryable
tool_choice
errorCategory
questions.why: — Attaching a publication or data-collection date to each extracted value lets downstream synthesis recognize a legitimate change over time rather than flag a contradiction. isRetryable (B), tool_choice (C), and errorCategory (D) are extraction-mechanics fields that say nothing about when the underlying fact was true.

questions.stem: Which best describes when retrying a failed extraction is NOT likely to help?
options: When the required information is genuinely absent from the source document entirely
When the model swapped two adjacent fields
When the validation error indicates a structural/format mismatch that's fixable through clearer instructions
When a nested array was flattened incorrectly
questions.why: — Retrying only helps when there's new information or clearer instruction to converge on; if the value was never in the source document, no retry can invent it. Swapped fields (B), flattened arrays (D), and structural/format mismatches (C) are exactly the error class a specific validation error message can fix.

questions.stem: An extraction schema requires stated_total and also asks the model to compute calculated_total from the line items. What is the purpose of including both?
options: Enabling downstream detection of semantic mismatches (the two numbers disagree) that schema validation alone wouldn't catch
Redundancy for its own sake
To satisfy tool_choice: "any" requirements
To reduce the number of required fields elsewhere
questions.why: — Requiring both the stated and a model-computed total creates a downstream check schema validation alone can't perform: if the two disagree, something is semantically wrong even in well-formed JSON. It isn't redundancy for its own sake (B), unrelated to tool_choice (C), and doesn't reduce required fields elsewhere (D).

questions.stem: A synthesis-style extraction task combines financial figures, narrative commentary, and technical specifications from a single source document into one structured output. How should each content type be rendered in the final structured output?
options: Only the financial figures should be kept; other content types should be dropped
Appropriately to its type — e.g., financial data as tables, narrative as prose, technical specs as structured lists
Uniformly as plain paragraphs regardless of content type
Entirely as a single JSON blob with no formatting distinctions
questions.why: — Financial figures, narrative, and specs carry different information shapes, and collapsing them into one uniform format throws away structure that's cheap to preserve and useful downstream. Dropping non-financial content (A) discards real information, and forcing everything into plain paragraphs (C) or an undifferentiated JSON blob (D) both erase distinctions the source document actually has.

questions.stem: A document-extraction pipeline needs to guarantee some structured output happens across three possible schemas, without the model ever responding with plain conversational text instead of calling a tool. Which tool_choice value should NOT be used here?
options: "auto"
Both B and C are acceptable depending on certainty about document type
"any"
A forced specific tool name, if the document type is already known
questions.why: — "auto" explicitly permits the model to answer with plain text instead of calling any tool, which is the one outcome this pipeline must prevent; "any" and a forced tool name both guarantee a tool call happens. B is a distractor implying conditionality where none exists — either "any" or a forced name alone already satisfies the guarantee.

questions.stem: 60. (Select TWO) Which two practices directly help prevent a model from fabricating values during structured extraction?
options: Marking fields nullable/optional when the source document may not contain them
Making every field required so the model is forced to always provide a value
Including few-shot examples showing correct null/absent-field handling
Increasing max_tokens substantially
questions.why: — Making fields nullable removes the pressure to invent a value just to satisfy a "required" constraint, and few-shot examples of correct null/absent-field handling model the desired behavior directly. Making every field required (B) increases fabrication pressure since the model must supply something, and a larger max_tokens budget (D) doesn't touch the underlying incentive to fabricate.
